name: Depth Priors and Initialization
text:
# Depth Priors and Initialization


## Overview
This family of methods addresses the ill-posed nature of single-view or sparse-view [NeRF](#1185-nerf-neural-radiance-fields.md) optimization by initializing or regularizing geometry using external depth estimates [G]. It sets itself apart from siblings like [Geometric Baseline Regularization](7475-geometric-baseline-regularization.md) by fusing perspective depth maps into a canonical panorama map via deformable alignment before training [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md], and distinguishes itself from [Depth-Supervised NeRF](8687-depth-supervised-nerf.md) by refining [radiance-field optimizations](#44-radiance-field-optimization.md) through external geometric priors rather than relying on multi-view consistency [14220-depth-supervision.md].

## Shared principles
All methods in this family integrate external depth estimates into the [differentiable volume rendering](#43-differentiable-volume-rendering.md) framework [Parent](8586-regularization-and-loss-functions.md). Gradients flow from the depth loss $\mathcal{L}_{\text{depth}}$ back through the rendered depth $\hat{\mathbf{D}}(\mathbf{r})$ to update the network parameters [G]. The rendered depth is computed as the expected distance along the ray:
$$ \hat{D}(\mathbf{r}) = \sum_{i=1}^N w_i t_i $$
where $w_i = T_i (1 - \exp(-\sigma_i \delta_i))$ are the rendering weights, $t_i$ are sample depths, and $T_i$ is the accumulated transmittance [G]. This expected depth serves as the differentiable geometric target for the supervision losses [G].

## Subtopics

### [Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map](8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md)
This method initializes the geometry of visible regions in a single-view NeRF using a 360-degree depth estimation pipeline, addressing the under-constrained optimization problem inherent to single-view reconstruction [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. It sets itself apart from sibling methods by explicitly fusing perspective depth maps into a canonical panorama depth map via deformable alignment before NeRF training, rather than relying solely on RGB consistency or post-hoc inpainting [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md]. Choose it when reconstructing scenes from a single panorama where standard monocular estimators fail on 360-degree inputs [8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md].

### [Depth Supervision](14220-depth-supervision.md)
[Depth supervision](#14220-depth-supervision.md) is a training technique that improves reconstructed geometry and reduces floating artifacts by providing depth priors derived from off-the-shelf monocular depth estimation models [14220-depth-supervision.md]. It distinguishes itself from sibling methods like [Single-view NeRF Training with Depth Map](8679-single-view-nerf-training-with-depth-map.md) by focusing on refining existing radiance-field optimizations through external geometric priors rather than relying solely on multi-view consistency or specific single-view architectures [14220-depth-supervision.md]. Choose it when training multi-view datasets where off-the-shelf depth models provide useful scale-consistent priors [14220-depth-supervision.md].

### Depth Supervision with Planar Architectural Depth Priors
**Definition:** Incorporates precomputed depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls into NeRF training to enforce geometric constraints on textureless planar surfaces [S1]. **Steps:** 1. Compute depth estimates for floor, ceiling, and walls using semantic segmentation [S1]. 2. Incorporate these priors into training with MSE and BoundL losses alongside photometric loss [S1]. 3. Train until convergence [S1]. **Parameters:** $\delta$ (BoundL tolerance): 1 mm. $\lambda_{\text{color}}$: 10 (bedroom), 1 (living room). $\lambda_{\text{depth}}$: 10 (bedroom), 1 (living room) [S1]. **Metrics:** RMSE of priors vs ground truth: 2.786 mm (bedroom), 3.201 mm (living room) [S1]. Converged in 120,000 iterations [S1]. **Comparison:** Faster convergence than photometric-only (120k vs 200k) and patch-regularization (120k vs 280k) methods due to depth supervision enabling quick identification of empty spaces, concentrating sampling on occupied regions, and providing a stronger optimization signal [S1].

## Background
The method originates from the challenge of improving geometric consistency for 360-degree [neural radiance fields](#4972-neural-radiance-fields.md) in indoor scenarios [S1]. It is used to address textureless surfaces like walls, floors, and ceilings, where photometric loss alone leads to "floaters" and cloudy artifacts [S1]. The approach incorporates precomputed architectural depth priors to enforce geometric constraints and accelerate convergence [S1].

## Sources
[S1] Improving Geometric Consistency for 360-Degree Neural Radiance Fields in Indoor Scenarios, https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.13710v1, fetched 2026-10-27
